title: TOP 10 Most Abandoned Places So Haunting Even Explorers Refuse to Return
fullText: In 1985, a lake in Argentina swallowed an entire town. The water rose for months. Hotels, churches, a slaughter house, all of it 10 m underwater. The town stayed submerged for 25 years. When the water finally pulled back, what came out was white, crystallized, coated in salt. And one man, 82 years old, moved back in alone. In another place, a farmer in Mexico was planting corn when the ground cracked open beneath his feet. Smoke poured from the fissure. By nightfall, a volcano had grown 6 m out of his cornfield. Within a year, it buried an entire village. The church tower is still visible, rising from a frozen sea of black lava. In the mountains of eastern Russia, the government disconnected the heating in a town of 12,000 people in winter at minus50. The residents walked out into the Siberian cold and never came back. Inside the apartments, a piano lid is still open. A globe on a teacher's desk still shows the Soviet Union. And in a resort town in Cyprus, 39,000 people fled in a single afternoon in 1974. The military sealed the perimeter with barbed wire. Hotel keys still hang on the rack behind the reception desk, one for each guest who never came back. That was 50 years ago. The wire is still there. This is our countdown of the 10 ghost towns abandoned overnight for reasons so terrifying most people cannot believe they are real. Stay until the end because number one is that drowned town in Argentina and the reason one old man chose to live there alone surrounded by salt and silence is something you need to hear for yourself. Before we start, drop a comment telling us where you are watching from right now. Last time we had viewers from over 50 countries. Let us see if we can beat that. Number 10, Kayakoy, Turkey. On Turkeykey's southwestern coast, between pinecovered hills, 500 stone houses sit in a valley. Doors, windows, fireplaces, staircases to secondf floor bedrooms. Two Greek Orthodox chapels with fresco still clinging to the walls. Nobody has lived in any of them for a hundred years. Kayakoy was a mixed Greek Turkish community for over two centuries. By the early 1900s, roughly 6,500 people shared the valley. Greeks on the hillside, Turks below. Shared markets, children from both communities in the same streets. According to records from the League of Nations, the coexistence was stable, not without tension, but functional. In 1923, the Treaty of Lausan ended it. A compulsory population exchange between Greece and Turkey. Roughly 1.2 2 million Greeks in Turkey forced to relocate. 400,000 Muslims in Greece sent the other direction. The architects of the treaty, primarily British and French diplomats, drew lines based on religion, not on whether the communities actually wanted to separate. The Greeks of Kayakoy were given weeks. They packed what they could carry. Some buried silverware and coins in their gardens. Parish records from the church of Taxi Arcus preserved by the Fetier Museum document families who listed their properties expecting to file claims upon return. They never filed those claims. Here is the detail that nobody expected. The Turkish families relocated from Greece to replace them arrived, looked at the 500 houses, and refused to move in. The Greek Orthodox layout felt wrong. The chapels with painted saints on every wall made them uncomfortable. According to ethnographic research compiled by the University of Anchora's Department of Folk Culture, the incoming families described the village as inhabited by ghosts, not literal ghosts, but the presence of another people's lives still visible in every doorframe and every wall painting. They built new homes in the lower valley instead. So 500 houses sat empty. UNESCO listed Kayakoy as a world friendship and peace village in 1988. The fresco in Taxi Arcus Chapel are still there, a little fainter every winter. Faces of saints painted by Greek artisans three centuries ago, slowly dissolving in a village that two governments emptied with a signature and a theory about where people belong. No bomb, no fire, no plague, just a treaty and 500 houses that have been holding their breath for a hundred years. Number nine, Agdam Azerbaijan. Spring of 1993, Agdam had 50,000 residents, apartment blocks, a 19th century mosque with a minouette visible from 10 km away, a bread factory that supplied the entire western region, a football stadium that held 12,000. By the end of July, the population was zero. The Nagorno Carabach conflict between Armenia and Azerbaijan had been building for years. When Armenian forces advanced on Agdam in July 1993, the city had no military defense. According to Human Rights Watch reports published in 1994, the civilian population fled in a mass exodus over roughly 48 hours. Families carried children on their backs. Farmers drove livestock down roads that were already jammed. Thousands walked east on foot with nothing but what they were wearing. The last families to leave reported passing through streets that were already silent, doors open, lights still on in apartments, a pot of food on a stove in one kitchen. According to a testimony collected by the International Crisis Group, left by a woman who stepped out to check on a neighbor and never came back for it. After the population fled, the city was dismantled. According to satellite analysis published by the American Association for the Advancement of Science, the destruction was not random. It was systematic. Wiring stripped, plumbing pulled, roofing removed, then the walls themselves block by block. The hospital, the school, the bread factory. Over the following decade, Abdom was reduced to a grid of foundations. International journalists who visited called it the Hiroshima of the Caucases. The only structure left standing was the mosque, its minouret rising over a flat expanse of rubble. Azerbaijan regained control in November 2020 as part of a ceasefire agreement. Recovery teams went in expecting ruins. What they found instead was a forest. In 27 years of emptiness, nature had swallowed the concrete. Full-grown malberry and walnut trees stood in living rooms. Root systems had cracked foundations. Grass covered the football pitch so completely that the goalposts were barely visible. A Reuters photographer who accompanied the first teams described finding a child's shoe in the rubble of a residential block. Still laced, sitting upright on a concrete slab as if someone had just stepped out of it. Reconstruction is underway. New roads have been laid. The mosque is being restored. But the 50,000 people who walked out in 48 hours scattered across Azerbaijon and built other lives. You can rebuild a city. You cannot reassemble the specific way a bread factory smelled at 5 in the morning when the first loaves came out. Number eight, Witten, Australia. Open Google Maps right now and search for Witten, Western Australia. Nothing. The town has been erased from every official map in the country. It is not underwater, not destroyed, not classified. Buildings standing, roads paved, street signs readable. The Australian government deleted it because the air will kill you. Whitenum was founded in 1937 as a blue asbestous mining town. The Whitnum Gorge mine operated by Australian Blue asbestous PTY Limited extracted crocidily, the most lethal form of asbestous fiber known to science. According to research published by the National Center for Epidemiology and Population Health at the Australian National University, crocidalite fibers are needle-shaped, thinner than a human hair, and small enough to penetrate deep into the plural lining of the lungs. Unlike other forms of asbestous, crocidily cannot be dissolved by the body's immune system. Once it enters the lungs, it stays. At its peak in the 1950s, roughly 20,000 people had lived or worked in Witten at various times. Miners operated underground with no respirators. The company's own internal reports from the 1940s, later obtained through litigation, acknowledged the hazard. Production continued. But here is the detail that makes Whitenum unlike any other contaminated site on Earth. The asbestous tailings, the crushed waste material from processing, were used as fill across the entire town. The Shy Council approved it. Schoolyards were paved with it. The local horse racetrack was surfaced with it. Children built castles and played barefoot in piles of blue asbestous dust after school. According to court documents from the 1988 Whitten litigation, parents described their children coming home covered in fine blue powder that they assumed was harmless. The mine closed in 1966. The dying started later and did not stop. A longitudinal study published in the British Journal of Industrial Medicine tracked former residents for decades. By 2012, the Western Australian Department of Health had documented over 2,000 deaths from metheloma, asbestosis, and lung cancer linked to witten exposure. 5-year-olds who built sand castles in 1955 were diagnosed with messyloma in 2005. 50 years between a sand castle and a death certificate. The government degazited Whitten in 2007, meaning it was officially removed from the register of towns. Road signs taken down, power cut, water cut. In 2022, the Western Australian Parliament passed legislation for compulsory property acquisition. Warning signs at the approach. Contaminated area do not stop. Three people still live there at last count. One of them, an elderly woman, told an Australian Broadcasting Corporation reporter that she had lived there for 40 years and was not going to let the government tell her where to die. The only town in Australian history officially deleted from existence. Not demolished, not evacuated, deleted. Because the thing that is killing people is invisible, weightless, and still floating in the air 60 years after the mine closed. Number seven, Xi Chang, China. In 1959, the Chinese government needed a hydroelectric dam in Jiang Province. The valley they chose had a city in it. Shiang, Lion City, founded during the Tang Dynasty around 621 AD, continuously inhabited for,300 years. According to provincial records preserved by the Xia Jang Cultural Heritage Administration, the city had carved stone archways at its five entrance gates, each aligned to a compass point of traditional Chinese geommancy, temples with handcarved dragon reliefs, a population of roughly 290,000 people. The government relocated every resident, every family, every business, every school. The process took months. According to accounts compiled by the Chandowa Lake Regional Administration, families were assigned new villages in surrounding areas. They were permitted to take personal belongings but not structural materials, houses, shops, temples. All of it was left standing. Then they opened the dam. Chando Lake, Thousand Island Lake, filled the valley. Xi- Chang sank beneath 40 m of water. The hilltops of the surrounding terrain became the thousand islands that give the lake its name. For 50 years, nobody went to look. The city was not a secret. Locals knew it was down there, but nobody had the equipment or the motivation to dive 40 m into a cold, dark lake to see what was left of a city that everyone assumed had been destroyed by submersion. In 2001, a tourism official named Chu Fang changed that. Working with Chinese National Geography magazine, he organized the first diving expedition to the submerged city. The team descended expecting silt, rubble, and collapsed walls. They came up and immediately requested a second team with underwater cameras. According to reporting by China Daily and subsequent archaeological assessments published by the Xiaang Provincial Institute of Cultural Relics and Archaeology, the city was almost perfectly preserved. The cold, oxygen- depleted water of Chanda Lake had acted as a natural preservative. Stone archways were standing. Dragon reliefs were sharp enough to trace with a finger. Wooden beams that would have rotted within years in open air were intact after four decades underwater. Streets were clear, building layouts recognizable. The five gates of Xi Chang still stand at the bottom of the lake, marking entrances to a city that no one uses. Fish swim through doorways. Algae grows on walls that once held calligraphy. Somewhere in the silt, there are objects that people sat down on the day they were told to leave. A cup on a table, a tool against a wall. 1300 years of continuous life, stopped on a government order in 1959, sitting in the dark 40 m down in a lake that most of the world does not know contains a city. If you are still watching, you already know this channel is for you. Hit subscribe and tell us in the comments which ghost town has stayed with you so far. The second half of this list goes to places that are harder to forget. Number six, KCO, Italy. In southern Italy in the Basilica region, a medieval town sits on a hilltop 500 m above the valley floor. It was first settled around 540 AD. By the medieval period, roughly 2,000 people lived in stone buildings that clung to a limestone cliff like barnacles on a ship's hull. KCO has been dying for 400 years, and it has not finished yet. The plague of 1656 cut the population nearly in half. According to records preserved by the arch dascese of Mata, the dead were buried in mass graves outside the town walls because the church cemetery could not hold them. The survivors rebuilt. Then the landslide started. The hill beneath KCO is composed of clayrich soil, a geological formation that shifts when saturated with water. According to surveys conducted by the Italian Geological Service in the 1950s, the entire hilltop had been experiencing slow subsidance for centuries. Buildings cracked, streets tilted, foundations separated from walls. The residents stayed. A major landslide in 1963 destabilized the eastern face. The Italian government ordered a partial evacuation. Roughly 1,800 people were moved to the valley settlement of Craco Pesciera. Some refused to go. They patched the cracks, braced the foundations with timber, kept living in a town the mountain was actively trying to shake off. A catastrophic flood in 1972 triggered a second collapse. This time, the remaining residents were forcibly removed. The road to KCO was closed. The town was sealed. When Italian preservation teams entered decades later to assess structural damage, they found something they did not expect. The town had not been stripped, not looted, not vandalized. Furniture sat in houses, kitchen tools on shelves, religious icons on walls. In one home, a pair of shoes by the front door positioned the way someone leaves them when they plan to put them back on in the morning. Hollywood found KCO before most of Italy did. Mel Gibson filmed scenes of The Passion of the Christ here. The James Bond production team used it for Quantum of Solace. According to the Basilica Film Commission, directors said they barely needed to modify the location. The real place was already more dramatic than anything a set designer could build. Geological surveys from the 1990s conducted by the University of Basilica's Department of Earth Sciences confirmed that the hilltop is beyond remediation. The clay base continues to shift. Some buildings have slid partway over the cliff edge, broken open, their rooms now facing a 300 m drop. Guided tours are restricted to specific routes because sections can collapse without warning. Four centuries of disasters, plague, landslides, floods, government evacuation orders. The people of KCO stayed through every single one until they were physically carried out. The buildings are still clinging to the cliff, cracked, leaning, sliding a few millimeters closer to the edge every year. A pair of shoes by a door still waiting. Number five, Humberstone, Chile. In the Ottakama Desert, the driest non-polar desert on Earth, there was once a town with a swimming pool. A proper one, full size, built in the middle of nothing, surrounded by salt flats stretching to every horizon. The workers who used that pool also had a theater that hosted touring opera companies, a market that imported European delicacies, electric street lights decades before most of Chile had electricity. All of it existed because of one chemical compound, sodium nitrate, salit. In the late 19th century, Chile controlled a near monopoly on natural nitrate, essential for both agricultural fertilizer and military explosives. Dozens of mining towns called Officina Salitas sprang up across the Atakama. Humberstone, originally founded as Officina La Palma in 1872, was one of the largest. According to records preserved by the Chilean National Monuments Council, the town had a hospital, a school, a church, a hotel, and the region's largest public swimming pool filled with desalinated water piped from the nitrate processing plant. The workers came from across Chile and from Bolivia, Peru, and Argentina. According to research by historian Sergio Gonzalez Miranda of the University of Arturo Pratt, the officina system created isolated self-contained communities that functioned as company towns. Workers were paid in features, tokens redeemable only at the company store. The prices at the company store were set by the company. The economics were circular by design. Then something happened in a laboratory 8,000 km away that erased it all. In 1909, German chemist Fritz Habber successfully synthesized ammonia from atmospheric nitrogen in Carls. His colleague Carl Bosch developed the industrial process. The Habber Bosch process, as it became known, allowed the production of synthetic nitrate at a fraction of the cost of mining it from the ground. According to economic data compiled by the Chilean Central Bank, Chile's share of global nitrate production dropped from over 50% in 1900 to less than 5% by 1940. Between the 1930s and 1960s, every officina in the Atakama shut down. Humberstone was abandoned in 1961. The last workers walked out. The pool drained. The theater went dark. UNESCO inscribed Humberstone as a world heritage site in 2005, noting that the nitrate towns represent the most complete testimony to a global industrial era that shaped modern agriculture and warfare. Today, visitors walk through Humberstone in silence. The pool is a cracked concrete basin bleached by 60 years of desert sun. The theater seats are dust. In the old company store, the shelves that once held imported olive oil and Portuguese wine hold nothing. A town that existed because of a mineral in the ground, killed by a formula written on a chalkboard in a city most of the workers had never heard of. Fritz Habber never knew about Humberstone. The workers of Humberstone never heard of Fritz Habber, and one destroyed the other without the two ever sharing a continent. Number four, Kadakchan, Russia. 500 km from the nearest city, Magadon Oblast, Far Eastern Russia. Winter temperatures -50° C. The sun disappears for weeks at a time. Kadikchan was a coal mining town of roughly 12,000 people. Built in the 1940s by prisoners of the Gulog system as part of Dalroy, the Soviet forced labor network in the Russian Far East. According to records from the Memorial International archive, the initial construction crews were political prisoners transported from western Russia in cattle cars. Many did not survive the first winter. The roads, the tunnels, the foundations of the town. All of it built on frozen ground by men whose names were recorded only as numbers. After Stalin's death, Kadikchan transitioned to civilian workers attracted by hardship bonuses, the Soviet term for extra pay offered to anyone willing to live where no one else would. By the 1980s, the town had apartment blocks, a school, a cultural center with a stage and a piano, a hospital, and central heating powered by the coal mined directly beneath the town. In 1996, an explosion in the mine killed six workers. The mine was permanently closed. What followed was not a gradual decline. According to reporting by Radio Free Europe, corroborated by Russian census data, the federal government made a decision that fits on a single line of a bureaucratic document. Services discontinued, heating disconnected, electricity shut off at minus50. The decision was administrative. The consequences were not. 12,000 people in a town with no alternative heat source, no road to anywhere warm, and a winter that would arrive in weeks. Residents were offered relocation assistance. According to accounts collected by Russian journalist Vasili Avchenko, who has documented abandoned Soviet towns extensively, the process was chaotic. Families left carrying whatever they could. many abandoned furniture, photographs, personal documents, anything too heavy for the walk to the transit point. The few explorers who have made the journey to Kadakchan in the years since describe something that is hard to process as real. The town is not ruined. It is paused. Propaganda murals on apartment walls, colors still vivid against gray concrete. A piano in the cultural center with its lid open. A Shopan nocturn on the music stand turned to the second page. A classroom with a globe on the teacher's desk, still showing the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics. A country that has not existed for over 30 years, sitting on a desk in a school where no bell has rung since 1996. And everywhere the ice. Every autumn, water seeps into cracks in the concrete. It freezes, expands, splits the wall a little wider, thaws in summer, seeps deeper, freezes again. Stelactites of ice hang from apartment ceilings, frost coats kitchen tables and children's beds. According to structural engineers who have assessed similar abandoned Soviet settlements for the Russian Academy of Sciences, this freeze thaw cycle is more destructive than decades of weather exposure. The buildings are not aging. They are being dismantled from inside by a process that runs on autopilot every winter. A shopan noturn on a music stand. A globe showing a country that does not exist. And a winter that takes the buildings apart piece by piece, not caring whether anyone is watching. Number three, Beichuan, China. May 12th, 2008. 2:28 p.m. local time. A magnitude 7.9 earthquake struck Sichuan province in central China. The rupture propagated along the long menshan fault for roughly 240 km according to the China earthquake administration. The city of Bichuan population roughly 30,000 sat in a narrow valley directly in the false path. Both sides of the valley collapsed inward at the same time. Official Chinese government figures 69,227 people killed across the region. In Beichuan alone, approximately 20,000, twothirds of the city's population, in 80 seconds. The Beichuan Middle School collapsed completely. According to reports compiled by the Shinua news agency, over 1,000 students and teachers were inside at the time of the quake. Roughly 800 died. One rescue worker told a journalist from Southern Weekend magazine that when his team reached the rubble of the school, they could hear a mobile phone ringing underneath. It rang for 3 days before the battery died. They never reached whoever was carrying it. Rescue teams pulled survivors from the wreckage for weeks. A woman was extracted from a collapsed apartment building after being trapped for over 100 hours. According to her account published in China Youth Daily, she stayed conscious by listening to her neighbors talking in the darkness around her. She could hear voices through the concrete. people trapped in adjacent apartments calling out, talking to each other to stay awake. Over the hours, the voices went silent one by one. The Chinese state council made an extraordinary decision. Beichuan would not be rebuilt. Not a single wall repaired, not a single street cleared. The entire city, collapsed buildings, buried roads, landslide scars, preserved exactly as the earthquake left it. A new Beichuan was constructed 20 km away on stable ground. Survivors were relocated. Old Beichuan was sealed behind walls and designated as the National Earthquake Memorial. Visitors today enter through a gate. The silence is immediate. Buildings lean against each other at angles that look staged for a film set and are not. Apartment blocks split in half. Rooms exposed to the open air. Furniture on floors tilted at 45°. A child's backpack hangs from a hook on a wall that is no longer vertical. There is a clock tower near the center. It stopped at 2:28 p.m. It has not been restarted. It will not be. In the ruins of the middle school, there are flowers, fresh flowers. They are replaced regularly. No organization coordinates this. According to Beichuan memorial management staff interviewed by the paper in 2023, parents simply come. Some drive hours. They place flowers at the perimeter of the school rubble and stand there. Sometimes for minutes, sometimes for an afternoon. 18 years later, the clock tower, the backpack on the hook, the phone that rang for three days, and the flowers that keep appearing at a school that has been rubble for almost two decades, placed by people whose children never came home from a Monday in May. Number two, Verosia, Famagusta, Cyprus. In the early 1970s, Verroa was one of the most exclusive beach resorts in the Mediterranean. Elizabeth Taylor stayed at its hotels. Breijit Bardaux sunbathed on its sand. Richard Burton drank at its bars. According to the Cypress Tourism Organization's records from 1973, Verocia's high-rise hotels were booked at over 90% capacity year round. Tour operators called it the French Riviera of Cyprus. On July 20th, 1974, Turkey invaded northern Cypress in response to a military coup on the island backed by the Greek Huta. Turkish forces advanced rapidly across the north. On August 15th, they reached Verosia. 39,000 residents fled south in hours. According to Republic of Cypress census records, the evacuation was almost entirely spontaneous. No official order, no organized transport. People grabbed what was closest. Some left on foot. Some drove. Many left doors unlocked, expecting to return by dinner. Turkish military forces sealed the perimeter. Barbed wire around every access road. Armed soldiers at every entry point. The United Nations Security Council passed resolution 550 in 1984 demanding that Verroia be returned to UN administration and that no one other than original inhabitants be permitted to resettle. That was 42 years ago. The resolution has never been implemented. Behind the wire, Verroia is frozen at August 1974. But frozen is not the right word. Frozen implies preservation. What happened in Verroia is closer to suspended decomposition. United Nations peacekeeping personnel who have entered the zone over the decades. Their accounts compiled in periodic UNFICP reports to the Security Council describe a place that is difficult to talk about in clinical terms. A car dealership with vehicles still in the showroom. 1974 price stickers on the windshields. A department store with merchandise on the shelves. Boxes faded. Packaging crumbled, but the products recognizable. A hotel lobby where room keys still hang on the rack behind the reception desk. One for each guest who never came back for their luggage. In one apartment, a table was still set, plates, cutlery, glasses, a calendar on the wall open to August 1974. In a bedroom, children's clothes folded in a wardrobe. The sizes suggest a child of about four. That child, if alive, is now in their mid-50s. The original residents of Verroia are in their 70s and 80s now. Some carry keys, metal keys to front doors they have not opened in half a century. In interviews with international media, the BBC, Alazer, the Guardian. Elderly men and women hold up these keys the way people in other contexts hold photographs of the dead. In 2020, the Turkish controlled government in northern Cyprus opened a small section of Verroia's beachfront to visitors. The European Union condemned the move. Greek Criate authorities called it a violation of international law. One of the first visitors was a woman who had lived there as a teenager. She stood outside the barbed wire perimeter and identified her old apartment building, 8th floor, third balcony from the left. She told a BBC reporter she could see her curtains, the same curtains her mother had hung in 1973, still there, still closed. She was not allowed to go inside. 39,000 people, 50 years, hotel keys still hanging on a rack, and a woman standing on a sidewalk in the Mediterranean sun, looking up at her mother's curtains through barbed wire. Because a war that lasted one month has kept her locked out for half a century. Number one, Via Epicquen, Argentina. Via Epiquen was a resort town in Buenosarees province built on the shore of Lago Epiquen, a saltwater lake 10 times saltier than the ocean. By the 1970s, up to 25,000 tourists arrived every summer season from Buenosire, 350 km east. Hotels, spas, thermal bathous, a railway station that brought visitors on packed weekend trains. According to the Buenosares Provincial Tourism Board records, the town was promoted as a health destination. The saltwater prescribed for rheumatism, psoriasis, and respiratory conditions. The permanent population was roughly500, families who ran the hotels, workers at the municipal slaughterhouse, teachers at the school, the kind of people who stayed through the quiet winters when the tourists left and the town returned to its real rhythm. bread deliveries, school bells, dogs barking at dusk. The town sat behind earthen embankments designed to hold the lake at a safe distance. Lago Epicquen is part of a chain of interconnected lakes in the Pompus region called the Encadanas Deoeste, the chained lakes of the west. The system is fed by rainfall across a vast agricultural basin. For decades, the embankments held. In the early 1980s, abnormally heavy rains raised the lake system far beyond recorded norms. By 1984, the water was pressing against the barriers. According to engineering reports later obtained by the Argentine newspaper Lassion, provincial engineers privately recommended a controlled release through drainage channels. The provincial government rejected the proposal. The cost was too high. They issued public asurances instead. On November 10th, 1985, the main embankment collapsed. The water did not crash through. It rose. According to municipal records from neighboring Caru and contemporary reporting by Lassion, the lake entered via Epiquen through the brereech steadily, advancing through the lowest streets first, ankle deep, then kneedeep, then at the doorsteps, then through the doors. Most of the population evacuated within 72 hours. Some went back for belongings. A butcher reportedly waited into his shop to retrieve his account ledger and had to swim out through his own front door when the water rose faster than he expected. The water did not stop. Over the following weeks, it climbed past ground floors, past second floors, past rooftops. By the early 1990s, Lago epiquen sat roughly 10 m above street level. Aerial photographs from 1993, preserved in the archives of the Instituto Geographico National show a flat gray expanse of water where the town had been. Nothing breaking the surface. Not a rooftop, not a steeple, not a treetop. For the 1500 permanent residents, the loss was not the kind where you lose a house and file a claim. The bakery counter your chin barely reached when you were five. The specific creek of the third step on your staircase. The way the afternoon light came through the kitchen window at a certain angle in December. All of it 10 m underwater with no reason to think any of it would ever surface again. Most resettled in Caru, 8 km east. The younger ones left for Buenosides. Over the years, Via Epequen became something old people mentioned, a town that used to exist. Occasionally, a retired tourist from the capital would bring up the salt baths they visited in the 1960s, and anyone under 40 had no idea what they were talking about. Then the climate shifted. A prolonged dry period starting in the early 2000s lowered the lake. By 2009, the tallest structures broke the surface. The water tower, the upper floors of the hotel castellar, then walls, doorways, streets, trees. What came out of that lake did not look like anything anyone had prepared for. 25 years of submersion in hypers saline water had coated every surface in thick white mineral crust. Trees that had been alive in 1985 stood as bleached skeletons, branches locked in the exact positions they had held when the water reached them, encased in salt deposits that gave them the texture of deep sea coral. Iron fences had bloated with rust and mineral into shapes that looked organic, like something grown rather than built. Cars sat on streets with dissolved tires but intact frames coated white like plaster casts of themselves. Researchers from the University of Buenosides who surveyed the emerging town beginning in 2010 documented objects preserved in ways they had not expected. A Coca-Cola bottle from the 1970s label legible beneath the mineral crust. Metal bed frames in hotel rooms still in position against walls coated in white. In the municipal slaughterhouse, meat hooks still hung from the ceiling rail. Each one encased in a crystallin shell in the exact working positions they had held on the last operating day. The hooks had not fallen. The rail had not buckled. The entire apparatus was frozen in salt like insects in amber. In a private home, a television set sat on a shelf, screen opaque with salt deposit, antenna extended as if someone had been adjusting the signal when the water came. In the school, desks sat in rows. The blackboard had dissolved, but its metal frame was still bolted to the wall. Photographers arrived first, then documentary crews. The Guardian, Leond, the BBC. The images were extraordinary. White streets under blue sky, skeletal trees casting long shadows on saltcrcustrusted pavement. A town that looked like a black and white photograph dropped into a color film. But the image that traveled farthest, the one that appeared in newspapers and broadcasts on three continents, was not a building or a tree. It was a man standing alone in the middle of a white street. 81 years old. His name was Pablo Novak. Novak was born in Via Epiquen, grew up there, worked there. According to an interview published by the Argentine news agency, Delam knew every family on every block by name. He was in his mid-50s when the water came. He evacuated with everyone else. Spent 25 years in Kadu, 8 km away, but a different place entirely. When the water receded, Pablo Novak went back not to visit, not to take photographs, to live. He found a small structure on the outskirts of the reemerged town that still had a roof. He cleaned out the salt debris, patched the holes, brought a bed, a stove, a chair, and a radio. Connected a water line from a functioning well, and moved in. The sole human resident of a town that had been at the bottom of a lake for a quarter of a century. Journalists found him within months. He became a minor international story. Camera crews from Bueno Zidis, from Madrid, from Tokyo. They filmed him walking the white streets alone, sitting in a chair outside his patched up door in the afternoon sun. Every crew asked the same question. His answer carried by AFP, Reuters, and the Associated Press in nearly identical form was this. I was born here. My parents are buried here. Everything I know is here. I do not want to die somewhere else. What is so strange about that? A journalist from the Buenosides Daily, Pahina 12, visited Novak and asked if he was lonely. Novak said no. He said the town was full of people. You just had to remember where they used to stand. He walked those streets every day. Past the slaughterhouse where he had worked, hooks still on the rail, past the hotel where his parents had taken him to dinner as a boy. past the church where he had been baptized. Walls standing, interior open to the sky, everything recognizable, nothing the same. A photographic negative of the town he remembered. Bleached white, crusted in mineral, silent except for the wind. Pablo Novak died in Via Epicquen in 2016 at the age of 89. He was still living there. After his death, no one replaced him. The house he had cleaned and patched is empty again. The lake is still receding. More structures surface every few months. A wall, a doorway, a staircase. Pieces of the town slowly ascending from the water and joining the rest of the skeleton in the sun. Somewhere under what remains of the waterline, there are rooms that have been dark since 1985.
